title: The RAG Report: Large Language Models in Legal Due Diligence
author: Ron Raini · Mike Kennedy · Elliot White · Kerry Westland

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s bounded-workflow framing and materially develops it through an applied M&A due-diligence use case. It treats document-set accuracy as the deployment constraint, tests existing techniques to improve general LLMs, and presents legally acceptable output as a prospective goal rather than evidence of autonomous legal competence.
qs: One of the main challenges of using GenAI technology ‘out of the box’ is how accurate the models will be when deployed to review large documents and document sets, compared to traditional machine learning tools and manual review.

This paper details our research into how the accuracy of LLMs can be improved using techniques that are already available and how this research underpins a Proof of Concept (PoC) multi-document review platform we are developing for an M&A transaction.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report materially extends the cluster’s proposition with a production-oriented due-diligence proof of concept showing that performance depends on provision-level task characteristics, bespoke retrieval and prompting, and workflow design. It also confirms that strong extraction results do not remove the need for human verification and senior legal judgment.
qs: The fact that customising a tool for a particular use case improves performance                                                                                       may not be a surprise; however, it strengthens our belief that investing time and GENERATION TESTS CONCLUSIONS                                                          resource into building solutions ourselves is a good approach.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between observed limitations and demonstrated benchmark success. It reports qualitative long-context degradation, cost and latency concerns motivating RAG, while treating embedding and prompt improvements as planned hypotheses rather than established reliability gains. It does not assess complete-task success or autonomous lawyering directly.

We will be experimenting with other, more advanced embedding models, as well as other providers and domain-specific (legal) embedding models and looking into training our own domain- specific embedding model.

st.t: Due diligence: Configuration drives extraction performance
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: its provision-extraction results vary materially with model choice, prompt workflow and provision type, while the tailored GPT4-32K RAG configuration performs best overall. It also treats explanations for weaker non-customisable tools as tentative rather than established causation.

st.t: Legal retrieval: Provision tuning beats universal rankings
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s retrieval proposition: provision-specific query optimisation substantially improves CUAD recall, but gains vary by provision, favouring selective optimisation. Its experiments measure retrieval of labelled text chunks rather than end-to-end legal analysis, so they do not establish universal legal competence or deployment reliability.
qs: We then tested the retrieval of all instances of a given Provision (as labelled in CUAD) and calculated the Recall@10 and Recall@20 over the entire collection of contracts.

The improvement         Optimised vs Non-optimised Retrieval varies depending on the specific Provision retrieved, showing that a use case and even a concept-specific optimisation strategy has a clear benefit.

kp.k: Optimisation substantially improved clause extraction performance
kp.d: Addleshaw Goddard reports that optimising retrieval and generation without training a new foundational model improved commercial-contract extraction. Its headline describes an increase from 74% to 95% in accuracy, but Appendix 2 identifies these endpoints as average F1 scores: full-context GPT4-Turbo with a first prompt versus RAG 10 GPT4-32K with improved prompting and follow-up. The appendix separately reports accuracy of 0.69 and 0.92. The narrative also reports 92% first-prompt F1 for the best configuration, whereas the appendix reports 0.88.
qs: We have shown that it is possible to optimise LLMs using a range of components to increase performance – in some cases by quite a margin.
Appendix 2 contains our full generation results in relation to all configurations and tools tested, including a detailed breakdown for each individual Provision.

kp.k: Evidence concerns extraction, not completed legal risk analysis
kp.d: Published results concern publicly available, annotated CUAD commercial agreements, not a demonstrated end-to-end diligence service. Retrieval experiments covered all 510 CUAD contracts; generation experiments used agreements between 40 and 60 chunks and nine provisions. Commercial agreements were the tested practice area, while risk identification and application to other areas remained further work. The authors report similar results in parallel testing with firm data, but the published results are CUAD-only.
qs: All the results shown in this paper are with respect to CUAD agreements only.
In this paper, we have focused on the retrieval and extraction aspects of the process, with risk identification currently ongoing.
This consisted of agreements between 40 and 60 chunks in length, which ensured that we did not run a full context review using our RAG approach by the inclusion of small documents.

kp.k: Success criteria permitted incomplete and related extractions
kp.d: The study evaluated extraction as classification against CUAD annotations. A true positive required at least 75% of the annotated provision and no hallucinations or misleading information. A true negative could include conceptually related provisions when the target provision was absent. The authors justified tolerance of related information by the planned downstream risk-identification stage, rather than requiring every extraction to be an exact, exhaustive match.
qs: A response containing an extraction of the target Provision.
A response stating ‘Not found’.
We evaluated all the configurations and third-party tools tested using the criteria described above.

kp.k: Hybrid retrieval delivered substantial, concept-specific gains
kp.d: The optimised method combined provision-specific vector queries with advanced keyword queries using proximity and boosting. Weighted retrieval recall rose from 81.31% to 97.28% at Recall@10 across all CUAD contracts; from 73.15% to 95.36% at Recall@10 for the 167 documents larger than 20 chunks; and from 83.07% to 97.95% at Recall@20 for the 71 documents larger than 40 chunks. These are improvements of 15.97, 22.21 and 14.88 percentage points respectively. Gains were larger for variable concepts such as exclusivity than for relatively standard governing-law clauses.
qs: 167 documents in CUAD are larger than 20 chunks
71 documents in CUAD are larger than 40 chunks.

This improvement of around 14% on average may not be as impressive as the other two scenarios, but it is still a clear indication of the effectiveness of our method, even when dealing with large documents.

kp.k: Chunking and limited context shaped extraction quality
kp.d: Testing three fixed-length chunking strategies on the 100 longest CUAD contracts led the authors to select 3,500-character chunks with 700-character overlaps either side. Under their restricted vector-search test, this achieved weighted Recall@1 of 36.62% and Recall@5 of 65.17%. The final configuration retrieved ten chunks and restored document order. Generation comparisons favoured targeted RAG context over full-document input; with GPT4-Turbo and follow-up, average F1 was 0.87 for full context, 0.89 for RAG 20 and 0.91 for RAG 10.
qs: Chunking Strategy 2: 3,500 characters long with an overlap of 700 characters either side.
This parameter deals with the order in which the retrieved chunks of each query are processed by the LLM.

kp.d: For RAG 10, GPT4-32K outperformed GPT4-Turbo on average: first-prompt F1 increased from 0.81 to 0.85, and follow-up F1 from 0.91 to 0.92. Across 18 provision-and-prompt comparisons, GPT4-32K performed better in 11, equally in four and worse in three. Testing used Azure OpenAI and the text-embedding-ada-002 embedding model; comparisons with Claude, Gemini and Llama, and more advanced embeddings, were planned rather than reported results.
qs: The specific LLMs that we used in these tests were GPT- 4-32K-0613 and GPT-4-Turbo-0125 through the Azure OpenAI service.
The only embedding model we used was OpenAI’s ‘text- embedding-ada-002’.

kp.k: Legal expertise improved prompts and search definitions
kp.d: The authors used clause banks and legal knowledge to construct queries, define provisions and address recurring errors, including confusion between effective date and agreement date. Added keyword-attention instructions improved follow-up F1 for cap on liability and exclusivity by 0.10 each and audit rights by 0.04, while change of control and licence grant were unchanged. They favour a targeted system prompt and more specific instructions nearer the question, cautioning that excessive detail can impair performance.
qs: Using a more elaborate and task-bespoke message does significantly improve the quality and depth of the model’s responses. However, we found that being too granular with task instructions has a detrimental effect on model performance
Using an Improved Provision Specific Prompt led to an increase in F1 score in three out of the five tested Provisions…

kp.k: Follow-up prompting improved recall without human re-prompting
kp.d: The authors report an average improvement of 9.2% across configurations from follow-up prompting, with some provision-level F1 improvements of 30% to 35%. Neutral requests to double-check generally repeated the original answer; directly accusing the model of missing information worked better. The proposed operational response is to automate this second request. Claims about emotive language are more tentative: its wording was not isolated in dedicated experiments.
qs: The Follow Up Prompt variation that improved performance the most was when we directly accused the LLM of missing relevant information.
Regardless of the output, we then immediately input a follow-up prompt which went back to the LLM alongside all of the above as well as the first response from the model.

kp.k: Bespoke extraction outperformed the tested third-party tools
kp.d: The best configuration's reported average F1 of 0.95 exceeded the traditional machine-learning extraction tool's 0.86 and the GenAI contract-review tool's 0.72. The machine-learning comparison used vendor-pretrained models without firm-specific training. The GenAI tool received the researchers' provision prompts, but its system settings could not be adjusted; it often paraphrased rather than reproduced text. The authors interpret these results as support for configurable, use-case-specific tools, not merely access to a general model.
qs: This illustrates the limitations of using general non-customisable tools and strengthens the case for investing time and resource into building bespoke solutions for specific use cases.

We have also discovered that through this optimisation process we can get better results than by using traditional Machine Learning Extraction Tools, although these solutions are closer in performance

kp.k: Earlier automation retained layered human review
kp.d: Describing its earlier machine-learning diligence work, the firm reports savings of around 50% of total diligence time and approximately 80% of manual review time. Paralegals or junior associates still checked extracted outputs, and senior lawyers subsequently identified risks and advised. The authors distinguish those realised historical savings from the newer ambition to automate more of the reporting workflow. They also state that the earlier percentage time saving did not increase when document volume increased.
qs: This is the period when it could truly be said that AI was being used on legal work.
For example, there would be an 80% time saving on the manual review of 100 documents, and the same 80% time saving when reviewing 10,000 documents.

kp.k: GenAI changes preparation requirements for bespoke extraction
kp.d: The authors argue that new provision types can be introduced through prompts rather than labelled examples and supervised model training. They qualify the speed advantage as clearest for bespoke extractions, since established machine-learning vendors already supply many pretrained concepts. They envisage progressing from extraction to answering risk questions, but the paper's reported comparative experiments concern the extraction stage.
qs: It allowed us to fail fast when querying documents, as we no longer faced a lead time to train a machine learning model.
An additional benefit with GenAI is the ability to get to the next stage of querying the extractions to identify risks

kp.k: Hallucination controls do not establish risk elimination
kp.d: The authors state that hallucinations did not pose a problem in their constrained extraction tests, potentially because of the task design and optimisation. Their safeguards included restricting answers to supplied excerpts, requesting verbatim extraction and explicitly allowing a 'Not found' response. They nevertheless warn that hallucination risk cannot be completely removed and that weak prompting or opaque third-party retrieval and system prompts can produce poor performance.
qs: In case you are unable to identify any Change of Control provisions, please respond with ‘Not found’.
Your answer must be based only on information appearing in the text excerpts, and you must avoid making any assumptions or providing speculative information.

kp.k: Internal platforms could embed expertise into diligence workflows
kp.d: The firm presents its proof of concept as a way to retain control over models, retrieval, prompts and risk parameters within its infrastructure. Its intended platform would classify deal-room documents, apply document-specific questions and produce draft diligence and risk reports with substantially less time and manpower. These are development objectives, not measured outcomes of the extraction study. Future work includes broader model testing, improved embeddings and chunking, risk evaluation and firm-wide deployment.
qs: Quickly classify, review and analyse all documents within a deal data room;
Apply pre-defined due diligence questions that are relevant to each document type;
Achieve this in a fraction of the time and manpower currently required to generate such reports.

kp.k: Prompting expertise may shift into system development
kp.d: The authors expect prompting to remain important but vary by user and task. Standard workflows can embed prompts in backend systems, reducing the need for lawyers to write them, while more sophisticated uses may require user control or visibility into instructions and available facts. Their recommendations centre on combining legal subject-matter expertise with technical development, rather than treating foundational-model capability alone as sufficient.
qs: For solutions that carry out standard tasks and workflows, building prompts into the backend system works well
LLMs may never reach a level where prompting doesn’t matter

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Raini, Kennedy, White and Westland argue that law firms can build bespoke, optimised RAG systems that substantially improve commercial-contract extraction without training a new model, and potentially support faster, less labour-intensive due diligence.
pts.d: The Addleshaw Goddard authors report an improvement described in the executive summary as average accuracy rising from 74% to 95%. Their generation results identify these endpoints as average F1 scores for full-context GPT-4-Turbo with a first prompt and optimised RAG10 GPT-4-32K with improved prompts and follow-up, respectively. They report that their bespoke configuration outperformed the tested machine-learning extraction tool (0.86 average F1) and GenAI contract-review tool (0.72). They attribute improvements to optimised retrieval, targeted prompts, limited relevant context and follow-up prompting, and report GPT-4-32K outperforming GPT-4-Turbo for this task. They argue that GenAI enables new bespoke extraction concepts without supervised model training and could extend extraction into risk identification. Their intended platform would classify and analyse deal-room documents, apply document-specific questions and draft due-diligence and risk reports with substantially less time and manpower. These end-to-end capabilities are objectives rather than the demonstrated scope of the extraction experiments. Separately, the authors describe earlier machine-learning projects as saving around 50% of total diligence-review time and approximately 80% of manual-review time.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is the firm's own CUAD-based retrieval and extraction testing, supplemented by implementation experience; prospective workflow benefits are not presented as measured end-to-end results.
pts.d: The firm-published research uses publicly annotated CUAD contracts. Chunking experiments used the 100 longest contracts and seven provisions. Retrieval experiments used all 510 contracts and longer-document subsets: optimised versus non-optimised weighted recall was 97.28% versus 81.31% for top-10 retrieval across all contracts, 95.36% versus 73.15% for top-10 retrieval in contracts exceeding 20 chunks, and 97.95% versus 83.07% for top-20 retrieval in contracts exceeding 40 chunks. These differences are percentage-point gains. Generation testing covered nine provisions in agreements 40–60 chunks long and compared ten configurations with two third-party tools. Outputs were classified against CUAD annotations: a true positive required at least 75% of a target provision and no hallucinations or misleading information; conceptually related extractions could be accepted when the target was absent. Appendix 2 reports the best configuration's average accuracy as 0.92, recall as 0.90, precision as 1.00 and F1 as 0.95, distinguishing the metrics underlying the headline. The text reports the improved-prompt first-response F1 as 0.92, whereas Appendix 2 reports 0.88. The machine-learning comparator used vendor-pretrained models, while the GenAI comparator used the firm's provision prompts but had system-level settings the researchers could not adjust. The authors report an average follow-up improvement of 9.2% across configurations and larger gains for some difficult provisions. Their statements about historical time savings derive from delivered projects, not the current generation benchmark. They describe emotive prompting as promising but say its wording was not isolated experimentally. Hallucinations are reported as not posing a problem in these constrained tests, rather than as a separately quantified general error rate.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern an October 2024 proof of concept for predefined commercial-contract provisions; broader risk analysis, firmwide rollout and transfer to other domains remain development plans.
pts.d: The reported results are conditional on task-specific legal and technical optimisation, not out-of-the-box LLM use. The selected configuration uses 3,500-character chunks with 700-character overlaps, hybrid advanced-keyword and vector retrieval, ten retrieved chunks in document order, GPT-4-32K, temperature zero, a 2,000-token response limit, a constant seed, targeted prompts and an automatic follow-up. The experiments concern retrieval and extraction, not validation of complete legal advice or due-diligence reports. Testing was confined to commercial agreements; application to real estate, employment, finance and tax is expected rather than demonstrated. The authors find that more context can degrade performance even within the available context window, and that excessive prompt detail can be detrimental. They qualify GenAI's speed advantage for adding concepts as clearest for bespoke extractions because existing machine-learning products already have extensive pretrained concept libraries. They acknowledge that hallucination risk cannot be eliminated completely. Plans for the following year include additional model families, embedding and chunking improvements, building the diligence offering and rolling it out across the firm. They also speculate that more domain-specific legal models may arrive over the next few years, without predicting a definite capability threshold or date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate implications concern M&A diligence teams, legal technologists and law-firm clients: more configurable extraction workflows, continued demand for subject-matter expertise and potentially reduced manual processing.
pts.d: The authors primarily address commercial-contract diligence within Addleshaw Goddard and comparable law-firm workflows. Internal innovation teams and lawyers supply the expertise needed to define provisions, refine retrieval queries and build reliable prompts; the proposed system embeds that expertise into repeatable workflows. Lawyers using the eventual platform may not need to draft sophisticated prompts themselves because developers can incorporate them behind the scenes, though the authors expect prompt awareness to remain useful for identifying errors and understanding limitations. In the historical machine-learning workflow, paralegals and junior associates verified extractions before senior lawyers assessed risk and advised clients. The new platform seeks to move beyond raw extraction toward answers and draft reports, but the paper does not quantify future junior-role displacement or establish that human verification can be removed. For law firms, the authors frame building internally as a means of gaining flexibility, control, reliability and affordability rather than relying entirely on third-party products. Clients are prospective beneficiaries of faster diligence and risk reporting, but no measured client-price reductions or market-share effects are offered. The source makes no concrete access-to-justice or profession-wide employment forecast.
